doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

chapter: Condon's circle and New York scene
title: Willie the Lion, jam sessions and Commodore Music Shop
summary: Jam sessions at Stuyvesant Casino and Central Plaza run by Jack Crystal, and meeting musicians at the Commodore shop.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I read somewhere that you had sat in or played for Willie “The Lion” Smith? Is that right?

Willie became one of my first mentors at the Central Plaza. Now I’m going back a couple of years to when I was about nineteen or twenty. The sessions were run in lower New York, New York City on the lower East Side. It was the Stuyvesant Casino and the Central Plaza. There are two big halls. And on Friday and Saturday night each hall would have their own jam session. One was run by Bob Maltz and the other was run by Jack Crystal, who is Billy Crystal’s dad. That’s why Billy’s got such a great influence in the music of today, I mean he just loved the times. And he’d be running around the hall there as a little kid, you know, and just absorbing all this stuff.
Didn’t his father sell records or something too?

Oh yeah. He was the manager of the Commodore Music Shop on 42nd Street. And that’s where I first met him. I was about fourteen or fifteen when I used to go in there and buy my first — not LPs, what am I saying — 78s. They cost a buck in those days. And that was pretty — a buck and three cents. And I met a lot of musicians going there and checking out their own records. Bud Freeman for one.

Really. JV; A funny guy. But I got to admire all these players and eventually in time in the future I wound up playing with most of them. And that was a big kick for me and a big thrill to admire these guys for years and then become their contemporaries.
